title: General Ability
attribution: Original CSS Vista learning exercises; not presented as authentic past-paper questions.

units.title: Numbers, place value & estimation
units.summary: Read numbers, work with negatives and check the size of an answer.

lessons.title: Place value
lessons.idea: A digit has a value because of its position. In 4,582, the 5 represents five hundreds.
lessons.rule: Expanded form adds the value of each digit.

example.problem: Write 6,307 in expanded form.
steps: There are no tens. Seven ones = 7.

exercise.prompt: What is the value of the digit 7 in 47,206?
exercise.explanation: The 7 is in the thousands column: 7 × 1,000 = 7,000.

lessons.title: Negative numbers
lessons.idea: On a number line, adding a positive number moves right. Adding a negative number moves left.
lessons.rule: Subtracting a negative is adding its opposite: a − (−b) = a + b.

example.problem: Calculate −8 − (−3).

exercise.prompt: Calculate −12 + 7 − (−4).
exercise.explanation: −12 + 7 = −5. Then subtracting −4 adds 4, giving −1.

lessons.title: Estimation
lessons.idea: Round first to predict the size of a calculation, then compute accurately when an exact answer is required.
lessons.rule: To round to the nearest ten, check the ones digit: 5 or more rounds up.

example.problem: Estimate 398 × 21 by rounding to 400 and 20.
steps: 398 is close to 400; 21 is close to 20.
This is an estimate. The exact product is 8,358.

exercise.prompt: Round 7,846 to the nearest hundred.
exercise.explanation: The tens digit is 4, so 7,846 rounds down to 7,800.

quiz.prompt: What is the value of 6 in 36,415?
quiz.explanation: The 6 occupies the thousands place.

quiz.prompt: Calculate −9 − (−14).
quiz.explanation: Subtracting −14 adds 14: −9 + 14 = 5.

quiz.prompt: Round 12,750 to the nearest hundred.
quiz.explanation: The tens digit is 5; increase the hundreds digit.

quiz.prompt: A temperature rises from −6°C to 8°C. What is the increase?
quiz.explanation: Final minus initial = 8 − (−6) = 14°C.

quiz.prompt: Estimate 49 × 202 by rounding to 50 and 200.
quiz.explanation: The stated rounded product is 50 × 200 = 10,000.

units.title: Basic calculation & order of operations
units.summary: Calculate accurately, handle brackets and use efficient mental methods.

lessons.title: Operation order
lessons.idea: Multiplication and division have equal priority and are processed left to right. Addition and subtraction then follow left to right.
lessons.rule: Brackets → powers → multiplication/division → addition/subtraction.

example.problem: Calculate 18 − 6 ÷ 3 × 2.

exercise.prompt: Calculate 24 ÷ 6 × 3 + 5.

lessons.title: Brackets and powers
lessons.idea: Brackets can change the calculation. A square means multiply the number by itself, not by two.
lessons.rule: Evaluate the bracket before applying its power.

example.problem: Calculate (7 − 3)² + 6.

exercise.prompt: Calculate 3 × (8 − 2)².
exercise.explanation: The bracket is 6; its square is 36; 3 × 36 = 108.

lessons.title: Mental calculation
lessons.idea: Split a difficult product into easy parts. This keeps the value unchanged because multiplication distributes over addition or subtraction.
lessons.rule: a(b + c) = ab + ac.

example.problem: Calculate 98 × 25.

exercise.prompt: Calculate 48 × 125 without a calculator.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 30 − 12 ÷ 4 × 3.
Calculate (5 + 3)² − 10.
quiz.explanation: The bracket is 8; 8² − 10 = 64 − 10 = 54.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 16 ÷ 4 ÷ 2.
quiz.explanation: Equal-priority divisions run left to right: 4 ÷ 2 = 2.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 99 × 37.
Calculate 7 + 2 × (9 − 4)².
quiz.explanation: The bracket is 5. Squaring gives 25; doubling and adding 7 gives 57.

units.title: Factors, HCF & LCM
units.summary: Use factors and multiples to group quantities and solve repeating-event problems.

lessons.title: Factors and primes
lessons.idea: A factor divides a whole number exactly. A prime number greater than 1 has exactly two positive factors: 1 and itself.
lessons.rule: Prime factorisation breaks a number into a product of primes.

example.problem: Factorise 84.

exercise.prompt: What is the largest prime factor of 90?
exercise.explanation: 90 = 2 × 3² × 5. Its prime factors are 2, 3 and 5.

lessons.title: Highest common factor
lessons.idea: The HCF is the largest number that divides each given quantity. It is useful when making the largest equal groups without a remainder.
lessons.rule: For prime factors, use only shared primes with the smaller exponent.

example.problem: Find the HCF of 36 and 48.

exercise.prompt: Find the HCF of 54 and 72.
exercise.explanation: 54 = 2 × 3³ and 72 = 2³ × 3². The shared product is 2 × 3² = 18.

lessons.title: Least common multiple
lessons.idea: The LCM is the smallest positive number divisible by every given number. It tells when repeating events coincide.
lessons.rule: For prime factors, take every required prime with the larger exponent.

example.problem: Two bells ring every 12 and 18 minutes. After ringing together, when do they next coincide?

exercise.prompt: Find the LCM of 15, 20 and 30.
exercise.explanation: The required prime powers are 2², 3 and 5. Their product is 60.

quiz.prompt: Find the HCF of 42 and 56.
quiz.explanation: 42 = 3 × 14 and 56 = 4 × 14; 14 is the greatest shared factor.

quiz.prompt: Find the LCM of 8 and 12.
Find the HCF of 24, 36 and 60.
quiz.explanation: 12 divides all three numbers; their shared prime powers give no larger factor.

quiz.prompt: Bells ring every 16 and 24 minutes and have just rung together. After how many minutes do they next ring together?
For two positive integers, HCF = 6 and LCM = 90. If one integer is 18, what is the other?
quiz.explanation: For two positive integers, product = HCF × LCM. The other integer is 540 ÷ 18 = 30.

units.title: Fractions
units.summary: Simplify, compare and calculate with fractions before applying them to word problems.

lessons.title: Equivalent fractions
lessons.idea: A fraction represents a number of equal parts. Multiplying or dividing both numerator and denominator by the same nonzero number preserves its value.
lessons.rule: Simplify by dividing both parts by their HCF.

example.problem: Simplify 18/24.

exercise.prompt: Simplify 21/35.
exercise.explanation: Divide numerator and denominator by 7: 21/35 = 3/5.

lessons.title: Addition and subtraction
lessons.idea: Fractions must describe the same-sized parts before they can be added. Use a common denominator, then combine numerators.
lessons.rule: a/c + b/c = (a + b)/c.

example.problem: Calculate 2/3 + 1/4.

exercise.prompt: Calculate 5/6 − 1/4.
exercise.explanation: Use denominator 12: 10/12 − 3/12 = 7/12.

lessons.title: Multiplication and division
lessons.idea: Multiplication takes a fraction of a quantity. Division by a nonzero fraction multiplies by its reciprocal.
lessons.rule: (a/b) ÷ (c/d) = (a/b) × (d/c), provided b, c and d are nonzero.

example.problem: Calculate (3/5) ÷ (9/10).

exercise.prompt: A tank is 3/4 full. One third of that water is removed. What fraction of the whole tank remains?
exercise.explanation: Two thirds of the existing water remains: (3/4) × (2/3) = 1/2 of the whole tank.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 3/8 + 1/6.
quiz.explanation: Use denominator 24: 9/24 + 4/24 = 13/24.

quiz.prompt: Calculate (4/7) × (21/8).
quiz.explanation: Cancel 21 with 7 and 4 with 8: the product is 3/2.

quiz.prompt: Calculate (5/6) ÷ (10/9).
quiz.explanation: Multiply by 9/10: 45/60 = 3/4.

quiz.prompt: Three fifths of a class of 45 students are present. How many students are absent?
quiz.explanation: Two fifths are absent: (2/5) × 45 = 18.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 2 + 3/4 − 1/2.

units.title: Decimals
units.summary: Understand decimal place value, conversions and accurate decimal operations.

lessons.title: Place value and conversion
lessons.idea: Digits after the decimal point represent tenths, hundredths and thousandths. Leading zeros matter to the value.
lessons.rule: A terminating decimal can be written over 10, 100, 1,000 and then simplified.

example.problem: Convert 0.375 to a fraction.

exercise.prompt: Convert 0.125 to a fraction.

lessons.title: Decimal operations
lessons.idea: Align decimal points for addition and subtraction. For multiplication, track the total number of decimal places.
lessons.rule: Multiplying or dividing by powers of ten changes place value.

example.problem: Calculate 2.4 × 0.15.
steps: The factors have three decimal places in total.

exercise.prompt: Calculate 3.6 × 0.25.
exercise.explanation: A quarter of 3.6 is 0.9; equivalently, 36 × 25 with three decimal places gives 0.900.

lessons.title: Division and rounding
lessons.idea: Scale both dividend and divisor equally to make decimal division easier. Round only at the requested final step.

example.problem: Calculate 4.8 ÷ 0.06.

exercise.prompt: Calculate 7.2 ÷ 0.08.

quiz.prompt: Convert 0.45 to a fraction in simplest form.
quiz.explanation: 45/100 simplifies to 9/20.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 0.6 × 0.4.
quiz.explanation: 6 × 4 = 24 with two decimal places: 0.24.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 5.25 − 1.8.
quiz.explanation: Write 1.8 as 1.80 and subtract to get 3.45.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 6.3 ÷ 0.09.
Round 3.476 to two decimal places.
quiz.explanation: The third decimal digit is 6, so increase the hundredths digit: 3.48.

units.title: Percentages
units.summary: Find parts, compare changes and reverse a percentage increase or decrease.

lessons.title: Percent of a quantity
lessons.idea: Percent means out of 100. Convert the percentage to a fraction or decimal before multiplying.

example.problem: Find 15% of 240.

exercise.prompt: Find 18% of 350.
exercise.explanation: Multiply 350 by 18/100 to get 63.

lessons.title: Percentage change
lessons.idea: A percentage increase or decrease is measured relative to the original value, not the final value.
lessons.rule: Percentage change = (change/original) × 100.

example.problem: A value rises from 80 to 100. Find the percentage increase.

exercise.prompt: A value falls from 250 to 200. Find the percentage decrease.
exercise.explanation: The fall is 50, and 50/250 × 100 = 20%.

lessons.title: Reverse and successive changes
lessons.idea: Successive percentage changes multiply their factors. Equal increases and decreases do not usually cancel.
lessons.rule: A 20% rise multiplies by 1.20; a 20% fall multiplies by 0.80.

example.problem: A price of 500 rises 10% then falls 10%. Find the final price.
steps: The net change is a 1% decrease.

exercise.prompt: After a 20% increase, a price is 900. What was the original price?
exercise.explanation: Final = original × 1.20, so original = 900 ÷ 1.20 = 750.

quiz.prompt: Find 12.5% of 320.
A value rises from 120 to 150. What is the percentage increase?
quiz.explanation: The increase is 30, measured against 120: 25%.

quiz.prompt: A price falls by 15% to 680. What was the original price?
quiz.explanation: 680 represents 85% of the original: 680 ÷ 0.85 = 800.

quiz.prompt: A quantity rises by 20% and then by 10%. What is the overall percentage increase?
quiz.explanation: 1.20 × 1.10 = 1.32, so the overall increase is 32%.

quiz.prompt: A quantity falls by 25%. What percentage increase restores its original value?
quiz.explanation: The remaining 75 must increase by 25. Relative to 75 this is 100/3%, approximately 33.33%.

units.title: Ratio & proportion
units.summary: Compare quantities, share totals and distinguish direct from inverse proportion.

lessons.title: Simplifying and sharing
lessons.idea: A ratio compares quantities in the same units. Add its parts before dividing a known total.
lessons.rule: For a:b, shares are total × a/(a+b) and total × b/(a+b).

example.problem: Divide 420 in the ratio 2:5.

exercise.prompt: Divide 560 in the ratio 3:4. What is the smaller share?
exercise.explanation: Seven parts share 560; each part is 80. Three parts give 240.

lessons.title: Direct proportion
lessons.idea: When the rate stays constant, twice the quantity costs twice as much. Start with the value for one unit.
lessons.rule: If y is directly proportional to x, y/x is constant.

example.problem: Five notebooks cost 450. What do eight cost at the same rate?

exercise.prompt: Seven identical items cost 840. What do eleven cost at the same rate?
exercise.explanation: One item costs 120, so eleven cost 1,320.

lessons.title: Inverse and compound proportion
lessons.idea: For a fixed job at a fixed rate per worker, more workers need less time. Not every situation is directly proportional.
lessons.rule: Equal workers × days stays constant for the same job.

example.problem: Six equal workers finish a job in 10 days. How long do 15 equal workers take?

exercise.prompt: Eight equally productive workers finish a job in 15 days. How many days do twelve take?
exercise.explanation: The fixed job needs 120 worker-days; divide by 12 to get 10 days.

quiz.prompt: Divide 720 in the ratio 5:7. What is the larger share?
quiz.explanation: There are 12 parts of 60; seven parts give 420.

quiz.prompt: A:B = 2:3 and B:C = 4:5. What is A when C = 30?
quiz.explanation: Match B: A:B:C = 8:12:15. C = 30 sets one part to 2, so A = 16.

quiz.prompt: Four metres of cloth cost 600. What do nine metres cost at the same rate?
quiz.explanation: The rate is 150 per metre; nine metres cost 1,350.

quiz.prompt: Ten equal workers need 18 days. How long do fifteen need for the same job?
quiz.explanation: 180 worker-days divided by 15 gives 12 days.

quiz.prompt: A map scale is 1:50,000. A distance of 6 cm represents how many kilometres?
quiz.explanation: 6 cm represents 300,000 cm = 3,000 m = 3 km.

units.title: Averages & weighted averages
units.summary: Recover totals, combine groups and understand how a mean changes.

lessons.title: Arithmetic mean
lessons.idea: An arithmetic mean shares the total equally across the observations. A mean is not necessarily an actual observation.
lessons.rule: Mean = total/count; total = mean × count.

example.problem: Find the mean of 6, 9, 11 and 14.

exercise.prompt: Find the mean of 8, 12, 15, 17 and 18.
exercise.explanation: The total is 70. Divide by 5 to get 14.

lessons.title: Missing and replaced values
lessons.idea: Use the original total to find a missing number or the effect of replacing one value. Changing one observation changes the total by the same amount.
lessons.rule: New mean = (old total − removed value + new value)/count.

example.problem: Five numbers have mean 20. Four sum to 76. Find the fifth.

exercise.prompt: Six values have mean 15. Replace a value of 9 with 21. Find the new mean.
exercise.explanation: The total increases by 12 from 90 to 102; 102 ÷ 6 = 17.

lessons.title: Weighted means
lessons.idea: Do not simply average two group means when their sizes differ. Weight each mean by its group size.
lessons.rule: Combined mean = (n₁m₁ + n₂m₂)/(n₁+n₂).

example.problem: Ten students average 60 marks; twenty average 75. Find the combined mean.

exercise.prompt: Eight values average 12 and twelve values average 17. Find their combined mean.
exercise.explanation: The totals are 96 and 204. Their combined total 300 divided by 20 is 15.

quiz.prompt: Find the mean of 4, 10, 14 and 20.
Five numbers average 18. Four total 64. Find the fifth.
quiz.explanation: The total is 90, so the missing value is 26.

quiz.prompt: Eight values average 25. A value of 12 is replaced by 36. Find the new mean.
quiz.explanation: The total rises by 24, increasing the mean by 3 to 28.

quiz.prompt: Groups of 15 and 5 students average 40 and 60 marks. Find the combined mean.
quiz.explanation: The total is 900 across 20 students; mean = 45.

quiz.prompt: Four numbers average 21. Add a fifth number to make the mean 24. Find the new number.
quiz.explanation: The new total is 120 and the old total is 84; the added number is 36.

units.title: Profit & loss
units.summary: Keep cost price and selling price distinct, and choose the correct percentage base.

lessons.title: Cost and selling price
lessons.idea: Profit is selling price minus cost price. Loss is cost price minus selling price. In standard profit/loss questions, the percentage is measured against cost price.
lessons.rule: Profit% = profit/cost × 100; loss% = loss/cost × 100.

example.problem: An item costs 800 and sells for 920. Find profit%.

exercise.prompt: An item costs 600 and sells for 690. Find profit%.
exercise.explanation: The profit is 90; relative to cost 600, this is 15%.

lessons.title: Finding the selling price
lessons.idea: Convert a target profit or loss into a multiplier of the cost price.
lessons.rule: Selling price = cost × (1 ± percentage/100).

example.problem: An item costs 1,250 and is sold at a 12% loss.

exercise.prompt: Find the selling price of an item costing 1,600 with a 25% profit.

lessons.title: Reverse profit and combined sales
lessons.idea: When selling price and profit% are known, divide by the profit factor. For several sales, compare total selling price against total cost.
lessons.rule: Cost = selling price/(1 + profit rate).

example.problem: An item sells for 1,080 at a 20% profit. Find cost.

exercise.prompt: Two items each cost 500. One sells at a 20% profit and the other at a 10% loss. Find total profit%.
exercise.explanation: Total selling price is 600 + 450 = 1,050. Profit is 50 on cost 1,000, or 5%.

quiz.prompt: An item costs 750 and sells for 900. Find profit%.
quiz.explanation: Profit is 150 on a cost of 750: 20%.

quiz.prompt: An item costs 1,200 and sells for 1,020. Find loss%.
quiz.explanation: The loss of 180 is 15% of cost.

quiz.prompt: Find the selling price of an item costing 960 at a 25% profit.
An item sells for 1,440 at a 20% loss. Find its cost.
quiz.explanation: 1,440 is 80% of cost. Divide by 0.80 to get 1,800.

quiz.prompt: Two items each sell for 600. One earns 20% profit and the other makes 20% loss. Find the overall loss%.
quiz.explanation: Their costs are 500 and 750. Selling total 1,200 loses 50 on 1,250: 4%. Equal selling prices do not give equal costs.

units.title: Discounts & successive price changes
units.summary: Work from marked price, apply successive discounts and connect discount to profit.

lessons.title: Marked price and discount
lessons.idea: Discount is the amount removed from marked price. Its percentage base is the marked price, not the selling price.
lessons.rule: Selling price = marked price × (1 − discount rate).

example.problem: A marked price of 2,000 has a 15% discount.

exercise.prompt: Find the selling price after a 12% discount on 2,500.
exercise.explanation: The customer pays 88% of 2,500, which is 2,200.

lessons.title: Successive discounts
lessons.idea: Each discount applies to the price remaining after the previous one. Adding the rates overstates the reduction.
lessons.rule: Final factor = (1 − d₁)(1 − d₂).

example.problem: Apply discounts of 20% then 10% to 1,000.

exercise.prompt: Find the equivalent discount% for successive discounts of 10% and 20%.
exercise.explanation: The final factor is 0.90 × 0.80 = 0.72; the discount is 28%.

lessons.title: Discount and profit together
lessons.idea: A discount can still leave a profit if marked price is sufficiently above cost. Apply the discount first and compare the result with cost.
lessons.rule: Profit% uses cost; discount% uses marked price.

example.problem: Cost is 800, marked price is 1,200 and discount is 25%. Find profit%.

exercise.prompt: Cost is 1,000 and marked price is 1,500. A 20% discount is allowed. Find profit%.
exercise.explanation: The selling price is 1,200; profit is 200 on 1,000, or 20%.

quiz.prompt: A price of 1,800 receives a 15% discount. Find the amount paid.
quiz.explanation: The customer pays 85% of 1,800 = 1,530.

quiz.prompt: A customer pays 960 after a 20% discount. Find marked price.
quiz.explanation: 960 is 80% of the marked price, which is 1,200.

quiz.prompt: Find the equivalent discount% for 25% followed by 20%.
quiz.explanation: 0.75 × 0.80 = 0.60, so the reduction is 40%.

quiz.prompt: Cost is 640, marked price is 1,000 and discount is 20%. Find profit%.
quiz.explanation: Selling price 800 gives profit 160 on cost 640, or 25%.

quiz.prompt: What marked price gives 20% profit on cost 900 after a 10% discount?
quiz.explanation: The required selling price is 1,080. Divide by 0.90 to get marked price 1,200.

units.title: Time & work
units.summary: Use rates for shared jobs, partial work and filling or draining tanks.

lessons.title: Work rates
lessons.idea: Treat a complete job as one unit. A worker who finishes in n days does 1/n of the job per day when the rate is constant.
lessons.rule: Work = rate × time.

example.problem: A worker finishes a job in 12 days. What fraction is completed in 3 days?

exercise.prompt: A worker takes 15 days. What fraction of the job is completed in 6 days?
exercise.explanation: 6 × 1/15 = 2/5 of the complete job.

lessons.title: Working together
lessons.idea: Add rates when independent workers contribute to the same job. Add their output, not the number of days.
lessons.rule: Together time = 1/(rate₁ + rate₂).

example.problem: A takes 6 days and B takes 12. Find their time together.

exercise.prompt: A takes 10 days and B takes 15. How many days do they take together?
exercise.explanation: Their combined rate is 1/6 of a job per day, so they need 6 days.

lessons.title: Partial work and opposing rates
lessons.idea: After part of a job is done, divide only the remaining work by the new rate. A drain subtracts from a filling rate.
lessons.rule: Net rate = filling rate − draining rate.

example.problem: A pipe fills in 8 hours and a drain empties in 24 hours. Find time to fill with both open.
steps: An empty tank fills in 12 hours.

exercise.prompt: A takes 12 days and B takes 18. They work together for 3 days, then B leaves. How many additional days does A need?
exercise.explanation: They complete 5/12 in three days. A finishes the remaining 7/12 at 1/12 per day, requiring 7 additional days.

quiz.prompt: A completes a job in 20 days. What fraction does A complete in 5 days?
quiz.explanation: Five days at 1/20 per day completes 1/4.

quiz.prompt: A takes 8 days and B takes 24. Find their time together.
quiz.explanation: Combined rate is 1/6, so time is 6 days.

quiz.prompt: A and B together take 6 days. A alone takes 10. Find B’s time alone.
quiz.explanation: B’s rate is 1/6 − 1/10 = 1/15; B takes 15 days.

quiz.prompt: A pipe fills in 6 hours while a drain empties in 18. With both open, how long to fill an empty tank?
quiz.explanation: Net rate is 1/9 tank per hour, so time is 9 hours.

quiz.prompt: A takes 9 days. B takes 18. A works alone for 3 days, then B joins. How many additional days finish the job?
quiz.explanation: Two thirds remain. Together the rate is 1/6, so the remaining time is 4 days.

units.title: Speed, distance & time
units.summary: Convert units, calculate journey averages and solve relative-speed problems.

lessons.title: Units and basic journeys
lessons.idea: Use consistent distance and time units. Speed is distance per unit time; time is distance divided by speed.
lessons.rule: km/h to m/s: multiply by 5/18. m/s to km/h: multiply by 18/5.

example.problem: A vehicle travels 150 km in 2.5 hours. Find speed.

exercise.prompt: Convert 72 km/h into m/s.

lessons.title: Average speed
lessons.idea: Average speed uses total distance divided by total time. Averaging two speeds is valid for equal travel times, not generally for equal distances.
lessons.rule: For equal distances at speeds u and v, average = 2uv/(u+v).

example.problem: Travel equal distances at 40 and 60 km/h. Find average speed.
steps: Times are 3 and 2 hours. Total distance 240 km divided by 5 hours = 48 km/h.

exercise.prompt: Travel equal distances at 30 and 60 km/h. Find average speed.
exercise.explanation: For equal distances, 2 × 30 × 60 ÷ 90 = 40 km/h.

lessons.title: Relative speed
lessons.idea: Opposite-direction closing speeds add. Same-direction closing speeds subtract. A train crossing a platform travels its own length plus platform length.
lessons.rule: Crossing time = total crossing distance/relative speed.

example.problem: A 120 m train at 54 km/h crosses a 180 m platform.

exercise.prompt: A 150 m train moving at 72 km/h crosses a 250 m platform. Find the time.
exercise.explanation: The crossing distance is 400 m and the speed is 20 m/s, giving 20 seconds.

quiz.prompt: How long to travel 180 km at 60 km/h?
quiz.explanation: Time = distance/speed = 3 hours.

quiz.prompt: Convert 90 km/h into m/s.
Travel equal distances at 40 and 80 km/h. Find average speed.
quiz.explanation: The harmonic mean is 160/3 km/h, approximately 53.33 km/h.

quiz.prompt: Two travellers start 270 km apart and approach at 40 and 50 km/h. When do they meet?
quiz.explanation: Closing speed is 90 km/h, so time is 3 hours.

quiz.prompt: A 180 m train passes a stationary pole at 54 km/h. Find the time.
quiz.explanation: The speed is 15 m/s, and only train length is crossed: 180/15 = 12 seconds.

units.title: Age problems
units.summary: Translate past and future ages into equations while keeping age differences constant.

lessons.title: Age differences
lessons.idea: Everyone’s age increases by the same elapsed time, so an age difference remains unchanged.
lessons.rule: If present age is x, age t years later is x+t and t years earlier is x−t.

example.problem: A is 28 and B is 16. What is their age difference six years later?

exercise.prompt: A is 31 and B is 19. Find their age difference eight years later.
exercise.explanation: Both ages increase by 8, so their difference remains 12.

lessons.title: Ratios of present ages
lessons.idea: Use a common multiplier for an age ratio. A known sum or difference then determines that multiplier.
lessons.rule: For ratio a:b, write ages as ak and bk.

example.problem: Ages are in ratio 3:5 and total 48.

exercise.prompt: Two ages are in ratio 2:5 and their sum is 49. Find the younger age.
exercise.explanation: Seven parts total 49, so one part is 7 and the younger age is 14.

lessons.title: Future and past equations
lessons.idea: Add or subtract time from each person separately before applying the stated future or past ratio.
lessons.rule: Present age relationships need not retain the same ratio over time.

example.problem: A is now 3 times B. In 10 years A will be twice B. Find B’s current age.
steps: x = 10, so B is 10 and A is 30.

exercise.prompt: A father is 4 times his son’s age. In 12 years he will be twice his son’s age. Find the son’s present age.

quiz.prompt: A is 40 and B is 25. Find their age difference after 9 years.
quiz.explanation: Their age difference stays 15 years.

quiz.prompt: Two present ages are in ratio 3:4 and total 56. Find the older age.
quiz.explanation: Each ratio part is 8; the older age is 4 × 8 = 32.

quiz.prompt: A is twice B and their ages sum to 45. Find B’s age.
quiz.explanation: If B = x, A = 2x; 3x = 45 gives x = 15.

quiz.prompt: A mother is 3 times her daughter’s age. In 8 years she will be twice the daughter’s age. Find the daughter’s current age.
quiz.explanation: 3x + 8 = 2(x + 8), giving x = 8.

quiz.prompt: Five years ago A was 4 times B’s age. A is now 45. Find B’s present age.
quiz.explanation: Five years ago A was 40 and B was 10. B is now 15.

units.title: Basic word problems & translating quantities
units.summary: Choose a variable, keep units consistent and check a story against its equation.

lessons.title: Build an equation
lessons.idea: Start with what the unknown represents. Translate each phrase in order and verify the answer in the original statement.
lessons.rule: “Five more than three times x” is 3x + 5, not 3(x+5).

example.problem: Five more than three times a number is 29. Find it.

exercise.prompt: Seven less than four times a number is 33. Find the number.

lessons.title: Count and cost
lessons.idea: A total number of items gives one relationship; a total cost gives another. Subtract a convenient all-one-price baseline.
lessons.rule: Extra cost divided by price difference gives the number of dearer items.

example.problem: Ten tickets cost 700. Adult tickets are 100 and child tickets 50. How many adult tickets?
steps: If all ten were child tickets, cost would be 500.
The extra 200 buys four upgrades of 50.
There are four adult tickets and six child tickets.

exercise.prompt: Twelve items cost 900. Each is priced at either 50 or 100. How many cost 100?
exercise.explanation: The all-cheap baseline is 600. The extra 300 represents six upgrades of 50.

lessons.title: Mixtures and conservation
lessons.idea: Mixing preserves the amount of the substance being tracked. A concentration refers to substance divided by total mixture.
lessons.rule: Substance before mixing = substance after mixing, unless some is added or removed.

example.problem: Mix 2 L of 20% solution with 3 L of 40% solution. Find concentration%.

exercise.prompt: Mix 4 L of 10% solution with 6 L of 30% solution. Find the final concentration%.
exercise.explanation: There are 0.4 + 1.8 = 2.2 L of the tracked substance in 10 L, giving 22%.

quiz.prompt: Three less than twice a number equals 17. Find the number.
quiz.explanation: 2x − 3 = 17 gives x = 10.

quiz.prompt: Three consecutive integers total 72. Find the middle integer.
quiz.explanation: The values are x−1, x, x+1, so 3x = 72 and x = 24.

quiz.prompt: Eight tickets cost 640. Adult tickets cost 100 and child tickets 60. Find the number of adult tickets.
quiz.explanation: The baseline is 480; extra cost 160 buys four upgrades of 40.

quiz.prompt: Mix 3 L of 20% solution with 2 L of 50% solution. Find concentration%.
quiz.explanation: The substance totals 1.6 L in 5 L, giving 32%.

quiz.prompt: Two numbers sum to 50 and differ by 8. Find the larger number.
quiz.explanation: Let larger x and smaller 50−x. Then 2x−50 = 8, giving x = 29.

units.title: Number series & patterns
units.summary: Apply stated sequence rules and check differences or ratios without guessing a unique rule from a short list.

lessons.title: Constant differences
lessons.idea: An arithmetic sequence changes by the same amount each step. Its nth term uses the first term plus n−1 changes.
lessons.rule: aₙ = a₁ + (n−1)d.

example.problem: Find the 10th term of 4, 7, 10, …, using a constant difference of 3.

exercise.prompt: A sequence starts at 5 and adds 4 each time. Find its 12th term.
exercise.explanation: There are eleven jumps from the first to the twelfth term: 5 + 44 = 49.

lessons.title: Constant ratios
lessons.idea: A geometric sequence multiplies by a fixed ratio. Count the number of multiplications from the first term.
lessons.rule: aₙ = a₁ × r^(n−1).

example.problem: Starting at 3 and doubling each term, find the 5th term.

exercise.prompt: A sequence starts at 2 and triples each term. Find the 5th term.
exercise.explanation: Four multiplications by 3 give 2 × 81 = 162.

lessons.title: Changing differences
lessons.idea: A finite list can fit many rules. In practice, use the specified difference pattern rather than claiming a mathematically unique continuation.
lessons.rule: Write consecutive differences, then test the stated rule.

example.problem: The sequence 2, 5, 10, 17, … uses successive odd differences 3, 5, 7, 9, … . Find the next term.

exercise.prompt: A sequence is 3, 7, 13, 21, … and its differences are successive even numbers 4, 6, 8, 10, … . Find the next term.
exercise.explanation: Under the stated rule, add the next difference 10 to 21, giving 31.

quiz.prompt: A sequence starts at 7 and adds 5 each step. Find its 8th term.
quiz.explanation: Seven differences give 7 + 35 = 42.

quiz.prompt: A sequence starts at 4 and doubles each step. Find its 6th term.
quiz.explanation: Five doublings give 4 × 32 = 128.

quiz.prompt: The nth term is n² + 1. Find the 7th term.
quiz.explanation: Substitute n = 7: 49 + 1 = 50.

quiz.prompt: The sequence 1, 4, 9, 16, … has nth term n². Find the next term.
quiz.explanation: The next term is the fifth square, 25.

quiz.prompt: Starting at 100, subtract 7 each step. Find the 9th term.
quiz.explanation: Eight subtractions give 100 − 56 = 44.

units.title: Algebraic expressions
units.summary: Substitute values, collect like terms and expand or factor expressions.

lessons.title: Substitution
lessons.idea: A variable stands for a number. Substitute its value with brackets, particularly when it is negative.

example.problem: Evaluate 3x² − 2x + 1 at x = −2.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate 2x² + 3x − 1 at x = −3.

lessons.title: Like terms and expansion
lessons.idea: Like terms have the same variable parts and powers. Apply multiplication to every term inside a bracket.
lessons.rule: 3x + 2x = 5x; 3x + 2x² cannot be combined into one like term.

example.problem: Simplify 3(x + 4) − 2(x − 1), then use x = 5.

exercise.prompt: Evaluate the simplified expression 4(x + 2) − 3(x − 1) at x = 6.
exercise.explanation: Expand to 4x + 8 − 3x + 3 = x + 11. At x = 6 the value is 17.

lessons.title: Factors and identities
lessons.idea: Factoring reverses expansion. A square of a sum includes a middle term; it is not just the sum of two squares.
lessons.rule: (a+b)² = a² + 2ab + b²; a²−b² = (a−b)(a+b).

example.problem: Calculate 51² using (50 + 1)².

exercise.prompt: Calculate 103² − 97² using the difference of squares.

quiz.prompt: Evaluate 5x − 2 at x = 7.
Evaluate x² − 3x at x = −4.
Evaluate 2(x + 5) + 3(x − 2) at x = 4.
quiz.explanation: The expression simplifies to 5x + 4. At 4 it equals 24.

quiz.prompt: Calculate 48 × 52 using a difference of squares.
For a = 3 and b = 5, calculate (a + b)².
quiz.explanation: The whole sum is squared: 8² = 64, not a² + b² = 34.

units.title: Equations: linear, simultaneous & quadratic
units.summary: Maintain equality, solve two unknowns and factor a quadratic with explicit answer conditions.

lessons.title: Linear equations
lessons.idea: An equation remains balanced if the same operation is applied to both sides. Expand brackets before collecting terms.
lessons.rule: Move toward an isolated variable, then substitute to check.

example.problem: Solve 3(x − 2) = 18.

exercise.prompt: Solve 5x + 7 = 42.
exercise.explanation: Subtract 7 to get 5x = 35; divide by 5 to get x = 7.

lessons.title: Simultaneous equations
lessons.idea: Two independent equations can determine two unknowns. Addition or subtraction may eliminate one variable.
lessons.rule: Eliminate, solve, then substitute into either original equation.

example.problem: Solve x + y = 10 and x − y = 4.

exercise.prompt: Solve x + y = 13 and x − y = 5. Enter x.
exercise.explanation: Add the equations: 2x = 18, so x = 9; y = 4.

lessons.title: Quadratic equations
lessons.idea: A factored quadratic equals zero when at least one factor is zero. Check all roots and apply any explicit condition.
lessons.rule: If (x−a)(x−b) = 0, then x = a or x = b.

example.problem: Solve x² − 5x + 6 = 0.
steps: Find numbers with product 6 and sum 5: 2 and 3.

exercise.prompt: For x² − 7x + 12 = 0, enter the larger root.
exercise.explanation: Factor as (x−3)(x−4) = 0. The roots are 3 and 4; the larger is 4.

quiz.prompt: Solve 4x − 9 = 23.
Solve 2(x + 3) = 5x − 9.
quiz.explanation: 2x + 6 = 5x − 9 gives 15 = 3x, so x = 5.

quiz.prompt: Solve x + y = 18 and x − y = 6. Enter y.
quiz.explanation: Subtract equations: 2y = 12, giving y = 6.

quiz.prompt: Solve 2x + y = 11 and x − y = 1. Enter x.
quiz.explanation: Add equations to get 3x = 12, so x = 4 and y = 3.

quiz.prompt: For x² − 9x + 20 = 0, enter the smaller root.
quiz.explanation: (x−4)(x−5) = 0, so the smaller root is 4.

units.title: Geometry, angles & area
units.summary: Use angle relationships, distinguish perimeter from area and apply right-triangle geometry.

lessons.title: Angles and triangles
lessons.idea: Angles on a straight line total 180°. Angles around a point total 360°. Interior angles in an ordinary plane triangle total 180°.
lessons.rule: Missing triangle angle = 180° − the two known angles.

example.problem: A triangle has angles 50° and 65°. Find its third angle.

exercise.prompt: A triangle has angles 35° and 75°. Find the third angle.
exercise.explanation: The two known angles total 110°. The remaining angle is 70°.

lessons.title: Perimeter and area
lessons.idea: Perimeter measures boundary length; area measures enclosed surface. Square units cannot be added directly to length units.
lessons.rule: Rectangle: area = length × width; perimeter = 2(length+width). Triangle area = ½ × base × perpendicular height.

example.problem: Find area and perimeter of a 9 cm by 4 cm rectangle.

exercise.prompt: A triangle has base 12 cm and perpendicular height 7 cm. Find its area.
exercise.explanation: Half of base × height is (12 × 7)/2 = 42 cm².

lessons.title: Right triangles and composite shapes
lessons.idea: The Pythagorean theorem applies to right triangles only. The hypotenuse is opposite the right angle and is the longest side.
lessons.rule: For a right triangle, c² = a² + b². Split composite areas into non-overlapping parts.

example.problem: A right triangle has perpendicular sides 6 cm and 8 cm.
steps: The positive hypotenuse length is 10 cm.

exercise.prompt: A rectangle is 15 cm by 10 cm. A 3 cm by 4 cm rectangular corner is removed. Find the remaining area.
exercise.explanation: Subtract the removed area 12 from the original area 150, giving 138 cm².

quiz.prompt: Two angles of a triangle are 42° and 68°. Find the third.
quiz.explanation: The third angle is 180 − 110 = 70°.

quiz.prompt: Find the perimeter of an 8 cm by 5 cm rectangle.
quiz.explanation: Add all sides: 2(8+5) = 26 cm.

quiz.prompt: A triangle has base 14 cm and perpendicular height 9 cm. Find area.
quiz.explanation: Area = ½ × 14 × 9 = 63 cm².

quiz.prompt: A right triangle has perpendicular sides 5 cm and 12 cm. Find its hypotenuse.
quiz.explanation: 5² + 12² = 169 = 13², so the positive length is 13 cm.

quiz.prompt: A square of side 10 cm has a non-overlapping 4 cm by 3 cm corner removed. Find the remaining area.
quiz.explanation: The original area 100 minus the removed area 12 gives 88 cm².

units.title: Circles: circumference, area & sectors
units.summary: Use radius correctly and relate sectors or rings to complete circles.

lessons.title: Radius and circumference
lessons.idea: Diameter is twice radius. Circumference is the boundary length of a circle; it uses length units.
lessons.rule: d = 2r; circumference = 2πr = πd.

example.problem: Find circumference when radius is 7 cm, using π = 22/7.

exercise.prompt: Find circumference of a circle with diameter 14 cm. Use π = 22/7.
exercise.explanation: Use πd, not 2πd: (22/7) × 14 = 44 cm.

lessons.title: Circle area and rings
lessons.idea: A circle’s area depends on radius squared. For a ring, subtract the smaller concentric circle from the larger one.
lessons.rule: Area = πr²; ring area = π(R²−r²).

example.problem: Find area for radius 7 cm, using π = 22/7.

exercise.prompt: A ring has outer radius 14 cm and inner radius 7 cm. Find its area. Use π = 22/7.
exercise.explanation: Subtract areas: (22/7) × (196−49) = 462 cm².

lessons.title: Sectors and arcs
lessons.idea: A sector represents its central-angle fraction of a full circle. Sector area and arc length use the same fraction but different full-circle formulas.
lessons.rule: Sector area = (θ/360)πr²; arc length = (θ/360)2πr.

example.problem: Find a 90° sector’s area with radius 14 cm, using π = 22/7.
steps: The sector is one quarter of the circle.

exercise.prompt: Find the arc length of a 60° sector of radius 21 cm. Use π = 22/7.
exercise.explanation: A sixth of circumference 132 cm is 22 cm.

quiz.prompt: A circle has radius 10 cm. Find its diameter.
quiz.explanation: Diameter is twice radius, so it is 20 cm.

quiz.prompt: Find circumference for radius 21 cm. Use π = 22/7.
Find area for diameter 28 cm. Use π = 22/7.
quiz.explanation: Radius is 14, so area is (22/7) × 196 = 616 cm².

quiz.prompt: Find area of a 90° sector with radius 7 cm. Use π = 22/7.
quiz.explanation: A quarter of 154 is 38.5 cm².

quiz.prompt: Find the ring area for outer radius 21 cm and inner radius 14 cm. Use π = 22/7.

units.title: Surface area
units.summary: Identify exposed surfaces and distinguish curved area from total area.

lessons.title: Cubes and cuboids
lessons.idea: Surface area adds the areas of exposed faces. A closed cuboid has three pairs of equal rectangular faces.
lessons.rule: Closed cuboid: 2(lw + lh + wh). Cube: 6a².

example.problem: Find total surface area of a closed cuboid 5 cm × 4 cm × 3 cm.

exercise.prompt: Find the total surface area of a cube of side 6 cm.
exercise.explanation: Each of six faces has area 36 cm²; total is 216 cm².

lessons.title: Cylinders and open containers
lessons.idea: A cylinder’s curved surface unrolls to a rectangle of width 2πr and height h. Include only the circular ends that actually exist.
lessons.rule: Curved area = 2πrh; closed total = 2πr(h+r); open-top container = 2πrh + πr².

example.problem: Find total area of a closed cylinder, r = 7 cm, h = 10 cm. Use π = 22/7.

exercise.prompt: Find surface area of an open-top cylindrical container, radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Use π = 22/7.
exercise.explanation: Include curved side 440 and one base 154: total 594 cm².

lessons.title: Cones and spheres
lessons.idea: A cone’s curved surface uses slant height, not vertical height. A sphere has one curved surface and no circular base.
lessons.rule: Cone total = πrl + πr². Sphere area = 4πr².

example.problem: Find total surface area of a cone with radius 7 cm and slant height 10 cm. Use π = 22/7.

exercise.prompt: Find surface area of a sphere of radius 7 cm. Use π = 22/7.

quiz.prompt: Find total surface area of a cube of side 5 cm.
quiz.explanation: Six square faces give 6 × 25 = 150 cm².

quiz.prompt: Find total surface area of a closed cuboid 8 cm × 5 cm × 3 cm.
quiz.explanation: Twice the face-area sum gives 2 × 79 = 158 cm².

quiz.prompt: Find curved surface area of a cylinder, radius 7 cm and height 12 cm. Use π = 22/7.
quiz.explanation: 2πrh = 44 × 12 = 528 cm²; do not add end faces.

quiz.prompt: Find curved surface area of a cone, radius 14 cm and slant height 15 cm. Use π = 22/7.
quiz.explanation: Curved area = πrl = (22/7) × 14 × 15 = 660 cm².

quiz.prompt: Find surface area of a sphere of radius 14 cm. Use π = 22/7.

units.title: Volume & capacity
units.summary: Calculate solid volume, convert capacity and use volume conservation.

lessons.title: Cubes, cuboids and capacity
lessons.idea: Volume measures occupied space in cubic units. Capacity conversions must cube the length conversion.
lessons.rule: Cuboid volume = lwh; cube volume = a³. 1 litre = 1,000 cm³; 1 m³ = 1,000 litres.

example.problem: Find capacity of a cuboid tank 50 cm × 40 cm × 30 cm.

exercise.prompt: A tank is 80 cm × 50 cm × 40 cm. Find its capacity in litres.
exercise.explanation: Volume is 160,000 cm³; dividing by 1,000 gives 160 litres.

lessons.title: Cylinders and displacement
lessons.idea: Cylinder volume is base area times vertical height. For a submerged object, the water-volume increase equals the submerged volume when no water spills.
lessons.rule: Cylinder volume = πr²h.

example.problem: Find volume of a cylinder with radius 7 cm and height 10 cm. Use π = 22/7.

exercise.prompt: Find volume of a cylinder with radius 14 cm and height 5 cm. Use π = 22/7.
exercise.explanation: Base area is 616 cm²; multiplying by height 5 gives 3,080 cm³.

lessons.title: Cones, spheres and scaling
lessons.idea: A cone has one third of the volume of a cylinder with the same base and vertical height. Scaling every length by k multiplies volume by k³.
lessons.rule: Cone = ⅓πr²h. Sphere = 4/3 πr³.

example.problem: Find volume of a cone with r = 7 cm and h = 12 cm. Use π = 22/7.

exercise.prompt: A cube has volume 27 cm³. Every edge is doubled. Find its new volume.
exercise.explanation: Doubling all three dimensions multiplies volume by 8, giving 216 cm³.

quiz.prompt: Find volume of a cube of side 4 cm.
quiz.explanation: Volume = 4³ = 64 cm³.

quiz.prompt: Convert 2.5 litres to cm³.
quiz.explanation: Each litre is 1,000 cm³, so 2.5 litres is 2,500 cm³.

quiz.prompt: Find volume of a cylinder, radius 7 cm and height 8 cm. Use π = 22/7.
Find volume of a cone, radius 7 cm and vertical height 9 cm. Use π = 22/7.
quiz.explanation: One third of 154 × 9 gives 462 cm³.

quiz.prompt: Find volume of a sphere with radius 3 cm. Use π = 3.14.
